extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, graduate students, and scholars of scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and characterize the criteria that define normal scientific practice: what counts as a legitimate problem, acceptable solution, and the role of paradigms, rules, instruments, and education in guiding research. Useful for historians/philosophers evaluating scientific traditions and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three classes of normal-science problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal research problems cluster into three kinds: determination of significant fact; matching of facts with theory; and articulation (refinement) of theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three classes exhaust most normal-scientific literature; examples include Coulomb’s measurement work and experiments distinguishing heating-by-compression theories. Articulation problems are simultaneously theoretical and experimental and serve to eliminate ambiguities of earlier formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science does not aim at major novelties
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical normal-science problems aim primarily to add scope and precision to the paradigm’s applications rather than to produce substantive conceptual or phenomenal novelties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes are usually within a narrow anticipated range and projects whose outcomes fall far outside that range are treated as research failures. Examples: wavelength measurements that only refine prior results; apparatus/instrument improvements appreciated mainly for enabling application of existing theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems must be puzzles (assured solvability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count as a puzzle (and thus as a legitimate normal-science problem) a problem must have an assured existence of a solution — it must be solvable in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to jigsaw or crossword puzzles: intrinsic importance is irrelevant; what matters is that a solution can be expected. Problems unlikely to be solvable (e.g., randomly mixed jigsaw pieces) do not function as puzzles and are not adopted as normal-science problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems must be constrained by rules limiting acceptable solutions and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A puzzle/problem must have rules that limit both what counts as an acceptable solution and the permissible steps to reach it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by jigsaw rules (all pieces used, plain sides down, interlock without forcing). Scientific analogues: apparatus must be analyzed in terms of established theory; theoretical solutions that would change the paradigm are not solutions to the old puzzle but redefine the problem (e.g., replacing inverse-square law would change the paradigm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible experimental results must be related to established theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental measurements are not meaningful until they are shown to correspond to theoretical quantities; instruments and their outputs must be analyzed and redesigned, if necessary, to correlate unequivocally with theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: early electron-scattering maxima had no significance until related to matter’s wave-like behavior; apparatus often must be redesigned so results can be assimilated into theory, otherwise colleagues may conclude nothing was measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit laws and theories function as primary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations expressed as scientific laws and theories set problems, bound admissible solutions, and serve as among the most binding rules in a research tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Newton’s laws constrained eighteenth- and nineteenth-century physics; laws of fixed proportions constrained chemistry; Maxwell’s equations and thermodynamics function similarly in modern contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental commitments constitute operative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred types of instrumentation and accepted manners of employing instruments form a significant body of rules that guide what problems are set and how they are solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include changing attitudes toward fire in chemical analysis, resistance to physical experimentation in physiology (Helmholtz), and the history of chromatography and X-ray discovery; such commitments can persist and shape research as strongly as laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-metaphysical commitments shape research agendas
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher-level conceptual or metaphysical commitments (e.g., corpuscularism) prescribe what entities and explanations are admissible and thereby direct the choice of problems and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corpuscular view after Descartes told scientists what entities existed and what explanations would count; this influenced chemistry, mechanics, optics, and heat by specifying which phenomena and problems to pursue (e.g., reactions seen as transmutations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-level commitments about aims and methods of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Commitments such as the aim to understand the world and to extend precision/scoping of order require detailed empirical scrutiny and refinement of observation or theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are commitments without which no one is a scientist: they motivate close empirical work and the refinement of techniques when pockets of disorder are observed; they are part of the rule-network guiding normal science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms are learned through exemplars (textbooks, lectures, labs) rather than abstract rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The paradigms of a mature scientific community are revealed in recurrent, quasi-standard illustrations — textbooks, lectures, laboratory exercises — and practitioners learn the trade by studying and practicing these exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific education teaches concepts, laws, and theories together with their applications; students acquire tacit knowledge and models by solving modeled problems and through laboratory practice rather than by learning an explicit abstract rule-set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms can guide research without an explicit body of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm can determine normal scientific practice even in the absence of a fully articulated, discoverable set of rules; paradigms often operate via family resemblances and tacit modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to abstract rules are difficult and often unsatisfactory; scientists may agree on exemplar achievements (paradigms) without agreeing on abstract rationalizations. References: Wittgenstein’s family resemblance, Polanyi’s tacit knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-provided criterion for problem selection (problems assumed solvable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm supplies the community’s criterion for choosing problems: those likely to have solutions within the paradigm’s conceptual and instrumental tools are selected; others are rejected or deemed metaphysical or another discipline’s concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, socially important problems that cannot be stated in paradigm terms may be ignored; paradigms insulate communities and focus practitioners on problems their tools can address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific education emphasizes modeling and tacit skill over explicit rule abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: From introductory courses through doctoral work, students learn theories in the context of applications; they gain ability to do research mainly by practice and exposure to solved problems rather than by abstracting explicit rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progression of assigned problems increases in complexity but remains modeled on prior achievements; mastery shows through successful problem-solving rather than verbalization of field-wide rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability of paradigms provokes explicit debates about rules and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When paradigms are insecure (pre-paradigm periods or revolutions), debates over legitimate methods, problems, and standards of solution intensify and may produce schools rather than consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: debates in optics and electricity, seventeenth-century chemistry, early nineteenth-century geology; transitions such as Newtonian→quantum mechanics evoked deep methodological debates; while paradigms are secure these debates are rare.
